questions.scenario: A manufacturer extracts purchase orders from 30 suppliers into its ERP with structured outputs. The schema declares `delivery_date` as `{ "type": "string", "format": "date" }` and lists it in `required`. Audits show that when a PO says "ASAP", "week 34", or nothing at all, the output still contains a precise date such as `2026-08-17`, which planners then trust. Of 1,200 audited POs, 9% had a delivery date that does not appear anywhere in the document. The ERP can store an empty delivery date and automatically flags those POs so a buyer calls the supplier. What is the most effective change?
options: Add a `pattern` regex for ISO dates to the field, so only well-formed values can be produced and the ERP never receives a malformed date.
Make `delivery_date` nullable, add a `delivery_date_text` field with the wording as written, and add few-shot examples where "ASAP" yields null.
Add a normalization rule: when only a week number is given, use the Monday of that week, and when no date is given, use the order date plus 14 days.
Keep the field required but add to the prompt: "IMPORTANT: never invent delivery dates that are not stated in the purchase order."
questions.why_correct: Un `string` obligatorio con `format: date` obliga a escribir una fecha válida aunque no exista. Hacerlo nullable le da al modelo una salida legítima ('no hay fecha'), el campo de texto conserva lo que dice el documento y los few-shot con null muestran cuándo usarla.

why_wrong.0: El formato ya era correcto; el problema es que el valor es inventado. Un regex no distingue una fecha real de una fabricada.
why_wrong.2: Es normalización que fabrica datos: el planner vería una fecha 'precisa' que nadie prometió. Normalizar es convertir lo que está, no rellenar lo que falta.
why_wrong.3: La instrucción choca con un schema que exige una fecha: el modelo queda entre la espada y la pared, y la forma del schema gana.

questions.rule: Dato que puede faltar → nullable + texto original + few-shot con null. Normalizá lo que está; no inventes lo que falta.
questions.source_quote: Allow Claude to say “I don’t know”: Explicitly give Claude permission to admit uncertainty. This technique can drastically reduce false information.

questions.scenario: A tax-tech startup extracts totals from receipts with structured outputs and four few-shot examples, all clean PDF receipts from large retailers with a "TOTAL" line at the bottom. After expanding to a new region, scans from street markets and handwritten receipts started arriving: the total appears as "A pagar" or "Importe", or is circled at the top of the page. On this new set, `total` comes back null in 38% of receipts where a human can see it clearly. The schema already makes `total` nullable, and the team wants to keep null for receipts that genuinely have no total. What is the most effective change?
options: Remove null from `total` so the field becomes a required number, which forces the model to locate a total in every receipt it processes.
Add an instruction listing synonyms for the total line ("A pagar", "Importe", "Amount due") and telling the model to look for it anywhere on the page.
Raise the effort level for receipts from the new region, so the model spends more reasoning on locating the total in unusual layouts.
Add few-shot examples from the new formats: a correct total from a market scan, one from a handwritten receipt, and one that truly has no total.
questions.why_correct: Los ejemplos actuales enseñan un único patrón ('TOTAL abajo'). Few-shot con los formatos nuevos muestran cómo se ve el total ahí, y uno sin total enseña cuándo el null es legítimo. Es la técnica que la guía asocia a nulls indebidos en campos que sí están en documentos con formatos variados.

why_wrong.0: Cambia nulls falsos por totales inventados en los recibos que de verdad no tienen total: violás la restricción y empeorás.
why_wrong.1: Ayuda algo, pero una lista de sinónimos no cubre layouts (un círculo arriba, letra manuscrita), y las instrucciones solas tienden a dar resultados inconsistentes; los ejemplos muestran el patrón.
why_wrong.2: Más razonamiento no le enseña cómo se ven estos formatos; el problema es de ejemplos, no de esfuerzo.

questions.rule: Nulls indebidos con formatos nuevos → few-shot con esos formatos (y uno con null legítimo).
questions.source_quote: Adding few-shot examples showing correct extraction from documents with varied formats to address empty/null extraction of required fields

questions.scenario: A food distributor extracts order lines from customer emails and PDFs into a schema with `quantity` (number) and `unit` (string). Inputs mix "2 doz eggs", "24 eggs", "1 case (12 x 1L)", "half a pallet" and "3 bx". Downstream, the warehouse system sums `quantity` per product and assumes it is always in single units; last month two orders shipped twelve times too little product. The team cannot change the warehouse system's schema, but it fully controls the extraction prompt and the extraction schema. What is the most effective change?
options: Instruct the model to convert every quantity to single units, keep the original wording in a `quantity_text` field, and add few-shot examples of tricky units.
Turn `unit` into an enum of `each`, `dozen`, `case`, `box` and `pallet`, so the warehouse always receives a unit from a known list that it can recognize and map.
Change `quantity` to `integer` in the schema, so the model is forced to return whole numbers and partial or informal amounts can't appear.
Add a post-processing step with regular expressions that detects words like "doz" or "case" in the source text and multiplies the quantity.
questions.why_correct: El sistema destino espera unidades sueltas, así que la normalización tiene que estar explícita en el prompt ('convertí todo a unidades'), con ejemplos de docenas, cajas y cantidades informales. El campo con el texto original permite auditar cada conversión.

why_wrong.1: Ordena la unidad pero no cambia la cantidad: el warehouse suma `quantity` sin mirar `unit`, y '2 dozen' sigue sumando 2.
why_wrong.2: Fuerza la forma, no el significado: '2 doz' sale como `2` igual, y 'half a pallet' pasa a ser un entero inventado.
why_wrong.3: Frágil frente a texto libre ('half a pallet', '12 x 1L'): cada formato nuevo es otro caso de regex. El modelo con instrucciones y ejemplos generaliza mejor.

questions.rule: Formatos variados → instrucciones de normalización explícitas + few-shot de los casos raros + campo con el texto original.
questions.source_quote: The effectiveness of few-shot examples for reducing hallucination in extraction tasks (e.g., handling informal measurements, varied document structures)

questions.scenario: A bank extracts 14 fields from commercial loan agreements of 60 to 120 pages (roughly 40k to 90k tokens each), including `governing_law`, `prepayment_fee_pct` and `change_of_control_trigger`. A legal audit found that 11% of `prepayment_fee_pct` values came from the wrong clause (a fee on a different facility in the same agreement), and some `governing_law` values matched the bank's standard template rather than the agreement itself. The fields are already nullable and the prompt already says to use only the document. Lawyers must be able to audit any value in seconds. Which change is most effective?
options: Split each agreement into 10-page chunks, extract the 14 fields from each chunk separately, and keep the first non-null value found for each field.
Add few-shot examples taken from short two-page term sheets, showing the expected value of each of the 14 fields in a clean, simple layout.
Ask Claude to first extract word-for-word quotes for each field into a `quote` property, then derive each value only from its quote, or null.
Add an instruction to double-check every value against the document, and to prefer the clause with the highest fee when several clauses match.
questions.why_correct: Documentos largos (más de 20k tokens) son el caso exacto donde la doc recomienda extraer citas textuales primero. Atar cada valor a su cita reduce los valores tomados de la cláusula equivocada o 'del template de siempre', y el abogado audita leyendo la cita.

why_wrong.0: 'Primer no-null' elige la cláusula que aparezca primero, no la correcta: justo el error de la fee de otra facilidad. Y se pierde el contexto entre chunks.
why_wrong.1: Ejemplos que no se parecen a los documentos reales (dos páginas vs. cien) no enseñan a navegar un contrato largo; los ejemplos tienen que reflejar el caso real.
why_wrong.3: 'Revisá dos veces' no deja evidencia auditable, y 'la fee más alta' es una regla inventada que puede elegir la cláusula equivocada.

questions.rule: Documento largo y valores que salen del lugar equivocado → citas textuales primero, valor derivado de la cita.
questions.source_quote: Use direct quotes for factual grounding: For tasks involving long documents (>20k tokens), ask Claude to extract word-for-word quotes first before performing its task.

questions.scenario: An online retailer's support agent runs on Claude Sonnet 5.5 for cost reasons and opens returns through a `create_return_ticket` tool whose `order_id` parameter is a required string. Logs show that when a customer describes a problem without giving an order number, 4% of tickets are created with plausible-looking IDs such as `ORD-58213` that match no order, so the warehouse emails return labels for orders that don't exist. Product will not move this flow to a more expensive model. When the order number is missing, the agent should ask the customer for it. What is the most effective change?
options: Add a `pattern` constraint to `order_id` that matches `ORD-` followed by five digits, so malformed IDs are rejected before the tool runs.
Make `order_id` nullable, say in the tool description that null means "not given by the customer", and add few-shot examples that ask for it.
Set `tool_choice` to force `create_return_ticket` on every turn where the customer reports a problem, so that the return flow always starts consistently.
Move the return flow to Claude Opus, which is much more likely to notice a missing required parameter and ask the customer for it.
questions.why_correct: Con un parámetro obligatorio y el dato ausente, la doc avisa que Sonnet puede 'inferir un valor razonable': esos son los IDs inventados. Nullable, una descripción clara de qué significa null y ejemplos que muestran 'pedir el número' le dan al modelo una salida correcta que no es inventar.

why_wrong.0: Los IDs inventados ya tienen el formato correcto (`ORD-58213`): un `pattern` no detecta que no existen.
why_wrong.2: Forzar la tool empeora: obliga a crear el ticket aunque falte el dato, y empuja todavía más a rellenarlo.
why_wrong.3: La doc dice que Opus lo detecta mejor, pero producto no acepta un modelo más caro: rompe la restricción.

questions.rule: Parámetro que el usuario puede no dar → nullable + ejemplos de qué hacer cuando falta. Nunca `required` a ciegas.
questions.source_quote: Claude Sonnet might ask, especially when prompted to think before outputting a tool request. But it might also infer a reasonable value.

questions.scenario: A travel-management company classifies 40,000 expense receipts a month into an enum `category` (`client_entertainment`, `team_meal`, `travel_meal`, `other`) with structured outputs. The system prompt contains a long paragraph defining each category. Agreement with the finance team's labels is 96% on clear cases but only 61% on ambiguous ones, such as a dinner with one client and three colleagues, or a breakfast at the airport hotel the morning of a client visit. The same ambiguous receipt sometimes gets different categories on different runs. Finance wants consistent decisions in the gray zone without rewriting the category definitions, which were approved by the auditors. What is the most effective change?
options: Add 2–4 few-shot examples of the ambiguous cases, each with the chosen category and a short note on why it beats the plausible alternative.
Add 25 more few-shot examples covering clear cases for every category, so the model sees many more instances of each label before classifying.
Extend each category definition with detailed rules and exceptions, so the system prompt spells out every edge case finance has run into so far.
Add an `uncertain` value to the enum and route those receipts to finance, so ambiguous cases are no longer forced into the four categories.
questions.why_correct: Las definiciones ya funcionan en lo claro; falla la zona gris. Pocos ejemplos dirigidos justo a esos casos, con la razón de por qué gana una categoría sobre la alternativa plausible, enseñan el criterio y el modelo lo generaliza a casos parecidos. Una explicación corta, no un volcado de razonamiento.

why_wrong.1: Más ejemplos de lo que ya sale bien no enseñan nada sobre lo ambiguo: suman tokens sin mover el 61%.
why_wrong.2: Choca con la restricción, y es la vía que la guía marca como insuficiente: las instrucciones detalladas solas dan resultados inconsistentes.
why_wrong.3: Esconde el problema: manda a finance buena parte de los casos ambiguos en vez de decidirlos de forma consistente.

questions.rule: Zona gris inconsistente → 2–4 few-shot de los casos ambiguos, con el porqué de la elección.
questions.source_quote: Creating 2-4 targeted few-shot examples for ambiguous scenarios that show reasoning for why one action was chosen over plausible alternatives

questions.scenario: A wholesaler ingests invoices from 300 suppliers in the US, the UK and Argentina. The extraction schema already declares `invoice_date` with `"format": "date"`, and every output is a well-formed ISO date. Reconciliation, however, shows that 7% of invoices from UK and Argentine suppliers have day and month swapped: "03/04/2026" became `2026-03-04` instead of `2026-04-03`. Each request already includes the supplier record, which has a `country` field. Auditors want the date exactly as printed preserved for disputed cases. What is the most effective change?
options: Replace `"format": "date"` with a `pattern` that only accepts `YYYY-MM-DD`, so the model is held to the ISO layout more strictly.
Ask the model to return dates in each supplier's native format instead of ISO, and let the ERP parse each country's format on import.
Add a rule keyed on the supplier's `country` (day-first outside the US), an `invoice_date_text` field with the printed date, and an ambiguous-date example.
Add an instruction telling the model to be especially careful with dates, and to double-check the day and the month before it writes `invoice_date` to the output.
questions.why_correct: `format: date` garantiza la *forma* ISO, no que el día y el mes estén en su lugar. Una regla de normalización explícita según el país del proveedor resuelve la ambigüedad, el texto original queda para auditoría y el ejemplo muestra el caso '03/04'.

why_wrong.0: Es el mismo error que ya tienen: más control de forma, cero control de significado. `2026-03-04` cumple cualquier patrón ISO.
why_wrong.1: Pasa el problema al ERP y pierde la normalización: cada país en un formato distinto es justo la inconsistencia que querés evitar.
why_wrong.3: 'Tené cuidado' no le dice cuál es la regla; sin saber que UK y Argentina van con el día primero, el modelo sigue adivinando.

questions.rule: El schema garantiza la forma, no el significado. La normalización necesita una regla explícita (y el texto original al lado).
questions.source_quote: Be specific about the output format and constraints you want.

questions.scenario: A university's research-synthesis system uses a subagent to extract study metadata (`sample_size`, `study_design`, `population`) from 3,000 papers with structured outputs. The papers vary widely: some report the sample size in the abstract, others only deep in the methodology, and many cite earlier studies inline ("a prior trial of 12,000 patients [14]"). Audits found that 18% of `sample_size` values were taken from a cited prior study instead of the paper being processed. `sample_size` is already nullable, and the prompt already says to use only the given paper. Which change is most effective?
options: Add a pre-processing step that keeps only the section titled "Methods" or "Methodology" and sends just that section to the extraction subagent.
Remove `sample_size` from the schema for papers without an explicit "N =" statement, and fill it in later from a public clinical trials registry.
Add an instruction stating that the sample size must describe the current study, written in capital letters at the top of the system prompt.
Add few-shot examples from varied paper structures, including one whose inline citation mentions a larger trial that must be ignored.
questions.why_correct: El error viene de estructuras variadas: el número citado se parece mucho al propio. Few-shot que muestran justo esa trampa (cita inline con un N más grande que no corresponde) y de dónde sale el valor correcto enseñan la distinción, y el modelo la generaliza a otros layouts.

why_wrong.0: Muchos papers no tienen una sección con ese título o reportan el N en el abstract; y las secciones de métodos también citan estudios previos. Recortás información y la trampa sigue.
why_wrong.1: Trae datos de afuera del documento y cambia el schema según el paper: más inconsistencia, y el registro no siempre coincide con el estudio.
why_wrong.2: La instrucción ya existe con otras palabras ('usá solo el paper'). Las mayúsculas no le enseñan a distinguir un N citado del propio.

questions.rule: Estructuras variadas que confunden → few-shot que muestran la trampa concreta y la extracción correcta.
questions.source_quote: Using few-shot examples to demonstrate correct handling of varied document structures (inline citations vs bibliographies, methodology sections vs embedded details)

questions.scenario: A procurement platform extracts supplier details from scanned invoices, including `vat_number` and `bank_iban`, both nullable. For invoices from very large, well-known vendors, auditors found that when the scan was cropped and the VAT number was missing from the page, the output still contained the vendor's publicly known VAT number. It was usually correct, but in two cases it belonged to a different subsidiary than the one issuing the invoice. The compliance team requires every value to come from the document itself. The prompt currently says only: "Extract the supplier's VAT number and IBAN." Which change best meets the compliance requirement?
options: Instruct Claude to use only information in the provided document, not its general knowledge, and to return null when a field isn't on the page.
Remove the vendor name from the input image before extraction, so the model can't recognize famous vendors and recall their known VAT numbers.
Keep the current behavior for well-known vendors, since the recalled VAT numbers are usually correct, and validate them against the national VAT registry.
Add a confidence score from 0 to 1 for each field and send any value with a confidence below 0.8 to a human reviewer before it is saved.
questions.why_correct: El modelo completa con conocimiento general. La doc tiene la técnica exacta: restringir explícitamente a la información de los documentos provistos. Con el campo nullable y permiso de devolver null cuando el dato no está en la página, la salida queda atada al documento, como exige compliance.

why_wrong.1: Tapa el síntoma y destruye un dato que también necesitás extraer (el proveedor); además, el modelo podría reconocerlo por otros datos de la factura.
why_wrong.2: Choca con la restricción: compliance exige que el valor salga del documento, y ya viste que el número 'recordado' puede ser de otra subsidiaria.
why_wrong.3: Un valor recordado de memoria puede venir con confianza alta: la confianza autoinformada no detecta que el dato no está en la página.

questions.rule: Datos que deben salir del documento → 'usá solo el documento, no tu conocimiento general' + null permitido.
questions.source_quote: External knowledge restriction: Explicitly instruct Claude to only use information from provided documents and not its general knowledge.

questions.scenario: An HR platform extracts fields from employment contracts using 12 few-shot examples. All 12 come from the same law firm's template, every field is filled in, and the examples are pasted into the prompt as plain paragraphs mixed in with the instructions. On real traffic, two problems appear: when a contract has no probation clause, the output still says `"probation_months": 3`, the value used in nearly every example; and in 2% of outputs the employer name is "Brightline Legal LLP", the firm from the examples, even though it appears nowhere in the contract. What is the most effective change?
options: Delete the examples entirely and rely on the JSON schema with nullable fields, since the examples are exactly what the model is copying values from.
Replace them with fewer, diverse examples from different templates, including one with no probation clause, each wrapped in `<example>` tags.
Keep the 12 examples but add the instruction "Never copy values from the examples" right below them, so the model treats them as format only.
Add 12 more examples from the same law firm's template with different employer names, so no single name appears often enough to be copied.
questions.why_correct: Dos síntomas, una causa: ejemplos todos iguales (el modelo aprende 'probation = 3' como patrón) y sin delimitar (se mezclan con las instrucciones). Ejemplos diversos, con un caso que da null, y envueltos en `<example>` para que se distingan de las instrucciones y del input.

why_wrong.0: Tirás la técnica más confiable para formato y consistencia; el problema no son los ejemplos sino que no son diversos ni están delimitados.
why_wrong.2: Parche parcial: puede bajar las copias literales, pero el sesgo de 'siempre hay probation' sigue, porque ningún ejemplo muestra el caso sin cláusula.
why_wrong.3: Más del mismo template refuerza el patrón; cambiar nombres no muestra el caso sin probation.

questions.rule: Few-shot: relevantes, diversos (incluí el caso null) y delimitados con `<example>`.
questions.source_quote: Diverse: Cover edge cases and vary enough that Claude doesn’t pick up unintended patterns.
